subject: Re: Integration follow-up: SDK/Auth/Response schema questions

Subject: Follow-up + a few architecture questions

Hi Marissa —

Thanks for the demo earlier. Priya and I did a quick sync after and have a handful of follow-ups so we can scope the integration work on our side. High level we loved the performance numbers and the routing idea to fall back to smaller models for non-critical paths. A few specific items where we need clarity so we can put together an internal effort estimate: 

1) SDK & auth: what SDKs should our backend team use for a Java (Spring) microservice? Do you support OIDC / short-lived creds or just API keys? Is there a recommended pattern for rotating keys during rollout?

2) Routing & model variants: can we pin a route to a fixed variant (e.g., redwood-llama-7b-8bit) and have automatic fallback to a cheaper variant on throttling? How are fallbacks configured?

3) Structured output / tool calling: we plan to use tool-calling to fetch DB rows and then format responses. Do you offer stable JSON schema enforcement or output types to avoid hallucinated fields?

4) Embeddings & reranker: we’ll run semantic search + rerank. Any advice on using embeddings for chunking vs. using the reranker endpoint? Are there limits on batch embedding size?

5) Request/response schema details: We do chat-style prompts and also some legacy completion endpoints. From a tokenization / max_tokens perspective what should we be aware of (stop sequences, streaming semantics, how streaming interacts with tools)?

We can share our tentative API shapes if that helps — sending you the mutual action plan shortly. Would appreciate a short doc or code sample we can show our backend lead.

Thanks,
Alex
Engineering Manager, Integrations
Acme Corp

Alex — thanks for the thoughtful list. I’m attaching a one-pager MAP (mutual action plan) and a short PDF with integration notes to get started (see attachments). I’ve looped in Dev from Solutions for the deeper SDK/auth and routing details.

Quick answers up front so your team can start estimating: 
- SDK: we have official SDKs for Python, Node, and Java; for Spring we recommend our Java client (sample below). We support API keys and OIDC (short-lived tokens via your IdP) for Private/Dedicated customers; hosted API supports API keys with recommended rotation via our Console.
- Routing: you can pin routes to a model variant, and define fallbacks by priority in the route config. We can share a sample route config and a policy that falls back to a cheaper variant on QPS or latency thresholds.
- Structured output: we support schema-guided generation plus function/tool calling; best practice is to use function signatures for strict typing and validate on the client.
- Embeddings: batch size recommendations depend on model; 512-2048 tokens per request commonly. For rerankers, we typically compute embeddings for candidates and then use a small cross-encoder reranker when you need high precision.

Next steps: Dev and I can host a 45-min technical call next week with your backend engineers to walk through the Java SDK, auth flow, and request/response examples. Does Tue or Wed morning PT work?

Best,

Subject: Re: Follow-up + a few architecture questions — SDK & Auth details

Hey Alex / Priya — glad the demo was useful. A few pragmatic notes from the engineering side to help your backend lead scope the work; happy to jump on a call and share a short Java sample repo.

SDK setup (Java/Spring):
- Use our Java client (artifact: com.redwood:inference-client). Minimal usage: create a client with an API key or OIDC token provider, then call chat() or embeddings() methods.
- Example (pseudo):
  - In Spring, wire a bean: new RedwoodClient.Builder().apiKey(System.getenv("RW_API_KEY")).region("us-west-2").build();
  - For OIDC, supply a tokenSource that refreshes before expiry; the client handles transient refresh errors.

Auth patterns:
- Hosted: short-lived API keys are not yet first-class; recommend rotating long-lived API keys and storing them in a secrets manager.
- Dedicated/Private: we support OIDC + role-based service accounts. OIDC is recommended for enterprise deployments (automated rotation, audit logs).

Routing & fallbacks:
- Route config example: primaryVariant: redwood-llama-7b-8bit, fallbackVariants: [redwood-3b-q4, redwood-1b-q4] with thresholds on latency/QPS.
- The routing policy is enforced at the gateway; you can set per-route SLOs and cost-priorities. Fallbacks are automatic once primary variant's queue crosses the threshold or if the variant returns 503.

Structured output / tool-calling:
- For deterministic JSON, use function/tool calling with explicit param schemas. The runtime will try to fill params; always validate server-side.
- For chat vs completion: chat endpoints are preferred for multi-turn state, tool-calling, and structured outputs; completion endpoints are still supported but lack the explicit function-calling contract in some models.

Embeddings & reranker:
- Batch embeddings up to ~2048 tokens per request for the larger embedding models; smaller models can do larger batch counts but watch memory.
- Reranker pattern: embed candidates, do ANN retrieval, then run a lightweight cross-encoder or reranker model on the top-K (K=10-50).

Attachments: I’ll upload a small Java sample and a route config snippet to the drive link Marissa shared.

—Dev
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@acme.com>, Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Follow-up + a few architecture questions — schema, tokens, streaming

Hi all — adding some engineering specifics on request/response schema and streaming semantics you asked about. I’ll keep it short and pragmatic.

1) Chat vs completion:
- Chat endpoints accept an array of messages (role/name/content). Use chat for multi-turn flows, tool-calling, and when you need to maintain role metadata. Completions can be simpler for single-shot prompts but don’t always include function-calling ergonomics.

2) Tokenization & max_tokens:
- All calls are limited by model max context (input + output). For example, if a model has 8k context and you send 6k tokens of prompt, you have ~2k tokens left for generation (subject to tokenization differences). Always calculate worst-case tokenization for user input; recommend truncation and explicit system-level summarization for long histories.
- max_tokens controls the maximum generated tokens. We recommend setting a hard upper bound in the client (e.g., 512 for chat responses) to avoid runaway costs.

3) stop sequences and streaming behavior:
- Stop tokens: you can pass stop sequences; the generator will attempt to stop when sequences appear. Note that partial streaming still sends chunks until the generator determines stop conditions, so your client should treat the final chunk with stop-handling logic.
- Streaming: our streaming API sends incremental deltas (token chunks) as they are generated. When using function-calling, we stream interim deltas and finalize with the function name + args. Expect that the final JSON may arrive across multiple chunks; assemble and then validate.

4) Structured output & validation:
- Best practice: use function signatures OR JSON schema + a validation pass. If you require strict determinism, run the model in constrained mode (max_tokens small, temperature 0) and validate server-side.

5) Practical defaults we often suggest for the first pass:
- chat endpoint, model: redwood-llama-7b-8bit (or redwood-3b-q4 for cost-sensitive paths)
- max_tokens: 512 (adjust per endpoint)
- temperature: 0.0-0.2 for structured outputs
- stop_sequences: ["\n\n", "END"] if you have a clear delimiter
- streaming: enable for UX-sensitive flows, but always reconstruct and validate final payload server-side

If you want, I can paste a short Java chat call snippet in the drive doc. Also happy to join the technical call next week to walk through streaming and function-calling edge cases (e.g., partial JSON fragments, retries).

—Rishi
Principal Engineer, Redwood Inference
